A written spec covering ingestion pipeline design (chunking, embedding, indexing), retrieval strategy (hybrid search, reranking), and generation layer (prompt template, context window).

sec-head.h2: When RAG is not the right choice

p: Part of a proper RAG pipeline development engagement is an honest assessment of whether a full retrieval-augmented generation pipeline is even necessary. If your data fits in a single prompt context or your questions are purely factual with no need for grounding, a simpler LLM call or a direct search may be faster and cheaper. See the RAG build agency services page for the fuller comparison.

faq-item.faq-q: What is the difference between a simple RAG pipeline and a multi-hop RAG?
faq-item.faq-a: A simple RAG pipeline retrieves documents for a single query and generates an answer. Multi-hop RAG breaks a complex question into sub-questions, retrieves iteratively, and synthesizes across multiple sources – ideal for domain-specific reasoning.

faq-item.faq-q: Do I need a RAG build agency, or can a freelance consultant handle my project?
faq-item.faq-a: Most RAG pipeline development projects are well within scope for a single experienced developer. An agency's advantage becomes relevant when a project needs multiple specialists across disciplines working simultaneously on a larger product.

faq-item.faq-q: How much does RAG pipeline development cost?
faq-item.faq-a: A single data source RAG pipeline typically runs $2,000 to $6,000. A full multi-source pipeline ranges from $8,000 to $30,000+ depending on complexity. Hourly consulting runs $75 to $150/hr.

RAG frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex are open-source and free under the MIT license. Embedding and LLM APIs incur costs based on usage, typically $0.10–$0.50 per 1M tokens for embeddings and $0.02–$0.10 per 1K tokens for generation.

faq-item.faq-q: When should I NOT use RAG?
faq-item.faq-a: If your data fits in a single prompt context (e.g., < 8K tokens) or your queries are purely factual with no need for grounding, a direct LLM call or a simple search may be faster and cheaper. RAG earns its complexity when you need to ground answers in large, dynamic corpora.
